newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Tietmeyer hopes mkts won't overreact on mark.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tietmeyer hopes mkts won't overreact on mark.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Thursday he hoped that the current correction of the deutschemark against the dollar would not go too far.

"For the most part, exchange rate developments are the result of corrections which were necessary. I hope now that it will not come to an overreaction," he told Spanish journalists after meeting Spain's Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato in Frankfurt.
"We are watching developments very carefully," he said, adding: "Central banks must watch the situation very closely."

The mark has depreciated sharply against the dollar this year, a move which analysts, including the German Finance Ministry and the Bundesbank, described as a correction from a situation where the dollar was considered too strong.

Many German officials now say the correction is complete. But, despite efforts by German Finance Minister Waigel this week to shore up the currency, the mark remains close to six-year lows against the dollar.
Tietmeyer said financial markets were "orienting themselves on their own estimation" of currency values and it was right for them to do so.
But he repeated several times during the interview that the situation should and would be carefully monitored.

The German cabinet said on Wednesday that it was in touch with its Group of Seven (G7) partners on the subject of the mark, but there has been no sign yet of coordinated action to support the currency.

On European economic and monetary union (EMU), Tiermeyer said he welcomed efforts by Spain and other southern European nations to reduce deficit and debt levels in the process towards the single currency.
"Spain has made great efforts and I am sure that it will make further progress," he said.

Asked whether he saw Spain, Italy and Portugal among the first group of EMU members, Tietmeyer said only that he hoped a large number of countries would meet the necessary criteria to ensure that the euro, due to be launched in 1999, would be stable.
"We would be happy when as many countries as possibible meet the conditions for a stable monetary union," he said.
